title: Server Actions
summary: **Server Actions** are async functions marked with `'use server'` that run only on the server and can be called directly from a form's `action` or from client code — letting you perform **mutations without writing API routes**, with built-in progressive enhancement and cache revalidation via `revalidatePath`/`revalidateTag`.

subtopics.title: The 'use server' directive
subtopics.explanation: A function (or whole file) marked `'use server'` becomes a Server Action: it always executes on the server, never ships to the client, and Next exposes a secure RPC endpoint for it automatically. You can define it inline inside a Server Component or in a separate file and import it into Client Components.

subtopics.title: Calling actions from a form
subtopics.explanation: Pass a Server Action directly to a form's `action` prop. On submit, Next serializes the FormData and invokes the action on the server — no fetch, no API route, no client JS required. This is the idiomatic way to do mutations in the App Router.

subtopics.title: Calling actions from client code
subtopics.explanation: Import a `'use server'` function into a Client Component and call it like any async function — Next turns the call into a POST to the action endpoint. Useful for optimistic updates, event handlers, or non-form interactions while keeping the logic on the server.
subtopics.example:
'use client';
async function onClick() { await toggleLike(postId); }

subtopics.title: Mutations without API routes
subtopics.explanation: Before Server Actions you wrote a route handler, fetched it from the client, parsed JSON, and handled errors by hand. Server Actions collapse all of that into one server function — the data layer is co-located with the component that uses it and there is no public REST surface to maintain.
subtopics.example: // No /api/todos route needed — the action IS the endpoint.

subtopics.title: Revalidating after a mutation
subtopics.explanation: After writing data the cached pages showing that data are stale. Call `revalidatePath('/todos')` to purge a route, or `revalidateTag('todos')` to purge every fetch tagged `'todos'`. The next request re-renders with fresh data. You can also `redirect()` to navigate after success.

subtopics.title: Progressive enhancement
subtopics.explanation: Because the action lives on a real form `action`, the form submits and works even before (or without) JavaScript hydrating. Once JS loads, Next upgrades it to a client-side request with no full reload. This is a major resilience win you get for free.

subtopics.title: Security & validation
subtopics.explanation: Server Actions are public POST endpoints, so treat every input as hostile: re-validate with a schema (e.g. Zod), check auth/authorization inside the action, and never trust hidden form fields or IDs. Anyone can invoke the action with arbitrary FormData.

subtopics.title: useFormStatus & useActionState
subtopics.explanation: `useFormStatus()` (in a child of the form) gives `pending` to disable buttons during submit. `useActionState(action, initial)` wraps an action to return `[state, formAction, isPending]`, letting the server return validation errors/messages that you render — the standard pattern for form feedback.

foundations.overview: Server Actions let you run server-side mutation logic by simply calling a function — from a form or from client code — without manually building, fetching, and parsing an API route. They are the App Router's first-class answer to 'how do I write data?', co-locating the mutation with the UI while keeping secrets and DB access on the server, and integrating directly with Next's caching so the UI stays fresh.
foundations.formalDefinition: A Server Action is an async function annotated with the `'use server'` directive that executes exclusively on the server. Next.js compiles it into a callable server endpoint that can be referenced from a form `action` attribute or imported and invoked from a Client Component, with arguments serialized over the network.
foundations.whyItMatters: Mutations are half of any app, and Server Actions remove an entire layer of boilerplate (route handler + client fetch + state management) while giving you progressive enhancement, type-safe calls, and automatic cache revalidation. They're a frequent advanced interview topic because they change the data-flow architecture of a Next.js app.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of a Server Action as a typed, secure RPC: you 'call a function' in your component, but it actually runs on the server. The form is the transport, `revalidatePath/Tag` is how you tell the cache the data changed, and validation/auth must live inside the action because the endpoint is public.
foundations.browserPerspective: Without JS, the browser does a normal form POST to the action endpoint and gets a fresh page back. With JS hydrated, React intercepts the submit, sends a background POST, applies the returned result, and revalidates affected routes — no full reload, and `pending` states drive the UI.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Creating/updating/deleting records (todos, comments, profile settings), submitting checkout or contact forms, toggling likes/follows, and any write that previously needed a dedicated POST endpoint.
foundations.businessImpact: Faster feature delivery (no parallel API layer to build and document) and more resilient forms (progressive enhancement) reduce both engineering cost and lost conversions from flaky client JS.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Co-locating mutations with components shrinks the codebase and eliminates a class of client/server contract bugs, but it shifts the burden of validation/auth onto the developer since each action is a public endpoint.
foundations.performanceImpact: Server Actions avoid an extra client round-trip of fetching-then-rendering, send less JS (logic stays server-side), and pair with targeted `revalidateTag` to refresh only what changed instead of refetching everything.
commonUseCases: Form submissions that create or update records
Mutations (delete, toggle, reorder) triggered from client event handlers
Revalidating cached pages after a write with revalidatePath/revalidateTag
Progressively-enhanced forms that work without client JavaScript

commonMisconceptions.myth: Server Actions are private because they only run on the server.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Each action is exposed as a public POST endpoint anyone can call with arbitrary input — you must validate and authorize inside the action.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You still need an API route to do mutations in Next.js.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Server Actions replace most internal mutation API routes; route handlers are mainly for external/public APIs and non-React consumers.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Data updates automatically after a Server Action.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Cached pages stay stale until you call revalidatePath/revalidateTag (or redirect to a revalidated route).

config.intro: Follow a form submission through a Server Action, mutation, revalidation, and UI refresh.

steps.name: Submit
steps.detail: The user submits a <form action={createTodo}>. Next serializes the FormData and POSTs it to the action's generated endpoint.

steps.name: Server runs
steps.detail: The 'use server' function executes on the server with access to the DB, secrets, and the session — none of which ship to the client.

steps.name: Validate & authorize
steps.detail: Inside the action you parse/validate input (e.g. Zod) and check auth, because the endpoint is publicly callable.

steps.name: Mutate
steps.detail: The action writes to the data store (create/update/delete). It can return a result object for the client to render.

steps.name: Revalidate
steps.detail: revalidatePath('/todos') or revalidateTag('todos') purges the affected cache entries so the next render is fresh.

steps.name: Refresh UI
steps.detail: Next re-renders affected segments (or you redirect). With JS, useFormStatus/useActionState drove pending and error states throughout.

codeLab.instructions: The illustrative action below does no validation or auth. Edit the printed code so it (1) checks the user is signed in, (2) validates the title is non-empty, and (3) revalidates after the write. Then Run.

hints: The action is a public endpoint — never trust the caller.
Return an error object for useActionState to render; throw for truly exceptional cases.

debuggingLab.title: The list doesn't update after adding an item
debuggingLab.symptom: Submitting the form creates the row in the database, but the rendered todo list still shows the old data until a hard refresh.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: The /todos page rendered with a cached fetch. Writing to the DB does NOT invalidate that cache, so Next keeps serving the previously-rendered (stale) data. The action must explicitly revalidate the path or tag that the list depends on.
commonMistakes: Assuming a mutation auto-invalidates the pages that read that data.
Calling revalidatePath with the wrong path (e.g. the action's path instead of the list route).
Tagging fetches inconsistently so revalidateTag misses some of them.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Add the correct revalidation call so the todo list re-renders with the new item.

theory.question: What is a Server Action and how does it differ from a route handler?
theory.directAnswer: A Server Action is an async function marked `'use server'` that runs only on the server and is callable directly from a form `action` or imported into client code — Next generates the RPC endpoint for you. A route handler (route.ts) is an explicit HTTP endpoint you define with GET/POST exports. Server Actions are the idiomatic way to do internal mutations co-located with components; route handlers are for public/external APIs and non-React consumers.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A server-only async function exposed as a callable endpoint via the 'use server' directive.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To do mutations without hand-building a fetch + API route + client state, while keeping logic and secrets on the server.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Next serializes the call's arguments (or FormData) to a generated POST endpoint, runs the function on the server, returns the result, and lets you revalidate the cache.

theory.whyImportant: It reshapes how data writes flow in a Next.js app and is a defining App Router skill that interviewers probe for.
theory.realWorldExample: A 'Create comment' form points its action at createComment; the action validates, inserts, and revalidateTag('comments') so the thread updates.

nestedTopics.title: Inline vs module actions
nestedTopics.explanation: Define inline in a Server Component, or in a 'use server' file to import into Client Components.

nestedTopics.title: Serialization limits
nestedTopics.explanation: Arguments and return values must be serializable; you can't pass functions or class instances.

followUps.question: Can a Client Component use a Server Action?
followUps.answer: Yes — import it from a 'use server' module and call it; Next turns the call into a POST to the action endpoint.

theory.question: How do useFormStatus and useActionState support Server Action forms?
theory.directAnswer: `useFormStatus()` reads the parent form's submission state (mainly `pending`) from within a child component, so you can disable the submit button and show a spinner. `useActionState(action, initialState)` wraps an action and returns `[state, formAction, isPending]`; the action receives the previous state plus FormData and returns the next state, which is the canonical way to surface server-side validation errors and success messages in the UI.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Two React hooks for driving form UX around Server Actions.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To handle pending and result/error states without manually wiring loading flags and fetch responses.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: useActionState binds the action so React tracks pending and threads the returned state back into render; useFormStatus exposes that pending to descendant components like a submit button.

theory.whyImportant: Form feedback (loading, errors) is essential UX, and these hooks are the standard, progressive-enhancement-friendly mechanism.
theory.realWorldExample: A signup form uses useActionState to show 'Email already taken' returned by the action, and a SubmitButton uses useFormStatus to disable while pending.

nestedTopics.title: Why a separate SubmitButton
nestedTopics.explanation: useFormStatus only works in a component rendered inside the form, so the button is usually its own component.

nestedTopics.title: Progressive enhancement
nestedTopics.explanation: Both hooks degrade gracefully — the form still posts without JS.

followUps.question: What was useActionState formerly called?
followUps.answer: It was previously experimental useFormState; useActionState is the stable name and also returns isPending.

scenario.question: A teammate exposes a deleteUser Server Action and trusts the userId sent from the form. What's the risk and how do you fix it?
scenario.directAnswer: Because the action is a public POST endpoint, any attacker can call it with an arbitrary userId and delete other users' data — there's a broken-access-control vulnerability. The fix is to never trust client-supplied identity: derive the user from the server session, authorize the operation (does this session own/permitted to delete this record?), and validate inputs with a schema before touching the database.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: An authorization flaw from treating a Server Action like trusted internal code.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Developers assume 'runs on the server' means 'private', but the endpoint is callable by anyone.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Auth/authorization and validation must execute inside the action; hidden form fields and IDs are attacker-controlled.

scenario.whyImportant: Server Actions move security responsibility onto the developer; missing checks are a real-world breach vector.

nestedTopics.title: Session-derived identity
nestedTopics.explanation: Read the acting user from the session, not from FormData.

nestedTopics.title: Input validation
nestedTopics.explanation: Schema-validate every field; reject unexpected shapes.

followUps.question: Does CSRF apply to Server Actions?
followUps.answer: Next includes protections (origin checks / action encryption), but you still must enforce auth and authorization yourself.

coding.question: Write a Server Action used with useActionState that validates input, persists it, and revalidates the list.
coding.thoughtProcess: The action must accept (prevState, formData) to work with useActionState. I'll authorize via the session, validate with a schema returning an error object on failure, write to the DB on success, revalidate the tag the list uses, and return a success state.
coding.lineByLine: createTodo takes (prevState, formData) so it slots into useActionState. It reads the user from the session (not the form), schema-validates the title and returns an error object on failure, writes the row, revalidateTag('todos') purges the cached list, and returns { ok: true }. The form binds formAction from useActionState; SubmitButton uses useFormStatus to disable while pending; state.error renders server-side validation messages.
coding.timeComplexity: O(1) plus the cost of the DB write.

alternativeApproaches.title: revalidatePath instead of tag
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Purge by route when fetches aren't tagged.

alternativeApproaches.title: redirect after success
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Navigate to a fresh route instead of returning state.

followUps.question: Why derive the user from the session instead of a hidden field?
followUps.answer: Hidden fields are attacker-controlled; the session is the only trustworthy identity source for authorization.

systemDesign.question: Design the data-mutation layer for a Next.js App Router product where most writes come from React forms but a mobile app and third-party webhooks also need to write. How do Server Actions fit?
systemDesign.directAnswer: Use Server Actions for all internal, React-driven mutations — they co-locate logic with the UI, give progressive enhancement, and integrate with cache revalidation. Put the actual business logic in a shared service layer (e.g. lib/services) that both Server Actions AND route handlers call, so there is one validated, authorized code path. Expose route handlers (route.ts) as the public/versioned HTTP API for the mobile app and webhooks, since those clients aren't React and need stable contracts, CORS, and auth tokens. This keeps a single source of truth for writes while serving both consumers idiomatically.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A layered mutation architecture separating transport (actions vs route handlers) from domain logic (a shared service).
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Different clients need different entry points, but you want exactly one place that validates, authorizes, writes, and revalidates.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Server Actions and route handlers are thin adapters; both call createTodoService(input, actor). Actions add revalidateTag after the service returns; route handlers shape JSON responses and CORS. The service owns validation, authorization, and persistence.

systemDesign.whyImportant: It tests whether the candidate avoids duplicating (and diverging) security logic across two endpoints and understands when each transport is appropriate.
systemDesign.realWorldExample: A SaaS where the web app's forms use Server Actions, the iOS app and Stripe webhooks hit /api/v1/* route handlers, and all of them funnel through the same lib/services functions.

nestedTopics.title: Shared service layer
nestedTopics.explanation: One validated/authorized function per use case, called by both transports.

nestedTopics.title: Cache coherence
nestedTopics.explanation: When a route handler or webhook writes, it must also revalidateTag so action-rendered pages stay consistent.

nestedTopics.title: Idempotency
nestedTopics.explanation: Webhook writes need idempotency keys; form actions can dedupe via unique constraints.

followUps.question: How do you keep the cache fresh when a webhook (not an action) writes?
followUps.answer: The webhook's route handler calls revalidateTag/revalidatePath for the affected data, or you use on-demand revalidation, so pages rendered via Server Actions stay consistent.

followUps.question: Why not expose Server Actions to the mobile app directly?
followUps.answer: Action endpoints are internal, unversioned, and React-serialization-oriented; a stable, documented route-handler API is the right contract for external clients.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Keep Server Actions as thin adapters that authorize, validate, call a shared service/domain function, and then revalidate. Define inline actions for simple Server-Component forms and module ('use server' file) actions when Client Components need them. Avoid putting business logic directly in the action so it can be reused by route handlers.
productionDeepDive.performance: Server Actions skip an extra client fetch-then-render cycle and keep mutation logic out of the JS bundle. Use revalidateTag for surgical cache invalidation instead of revalidating broad paths or using no-store everywhere, and pair with useOptimistic for instant UI feedback.
productionDeepDive.security: Every action is a public POST endpoint: derive identity from the session (never from form fields), authorize the specific operation, and schema-validate all input. Rely on Next's built-in origin/CSRF protections but don't depend on them for authorization. Rate-limit sensitive actions.
productionDeepDive.scaling: Actions run as server invocations (often serverless functions), so cold starts and per-call DB connections matter; use connection pooling and keep actions fast. Offload slow work (emails, image processing) to a queue and return quickly.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: Centralize validation schemas and the service layer; return typed state objects for useActionState so error handling is consistent. Co-locating actions with features keeps related code together and reviewable.
productionDeepDive.observability: Log action invocations with the acting user, validation failures, and revalidation calls. Monitor action latency and error rates separately from page renders, and trace which tags/paths get revalidated to debug stale-data issues.

caseStudies.problem: Mutation logic duplicated across API routes and client fetch code, drifting in validation and auth.
caseStudies.solution: Move internal writes to Server Actions backed by a shared service layer, revalidating tags after each write.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Less explicit HTTP surface and a learning curve, plus the discipline of treating actions as public endpoints.
caseStudies.lessons: Server Actions cut boilerplate and bugs, but only if validation/authorization is treated as mandatory, not optional.

projectBuilder.summary: Build the create/update/delete flows of the SaaS app entirely with Server Actions, including validation, auth, and cache revalidation.

Each action authorizes via the session and validates input with a schema
Forms show pending and error states via useFormStatus/useActionState
Affected pages refresh via revalidatePath/revalidateTag after writes
projectBuilder.architecture: Thin 'use server' actions in app/actions.ts call shared service functions in lib/services; forms live in Client Components using useActionState, and reads are tagged fetches that actions revalidate.

  todos/page.tsx        // reads tagged fetch, renders <TodoForm/>

steps.title: Define the service
steps.instructions: Write lib/services/todos.ts with validated, authorized create/update/delete functions.
steps.checkpoint: Service functions reject unauthorized or invalid input.

steps.title: Wrap with actions
steps.instructions: Create 'use server' actions that call the service and revalidate the 'todos' tag.
steps.checkpoint: Submitting a form writes data and the list refreshes without a hard reload.

steps.instructions: Use useActionState for errors and a SubmitButton with useFormStatus for pending.
steps.checkpoint: Invalid submits show server errors; the button disables while saving.

enhancements: Add useOptimistic for instant UI updates
Expose the same service via a versioned route handler for a mobile client
interviewQuestions: Why is revalidateTag preferable to revalidatePath here?
How do you keep the action secure when the userId could be spoofed?

keyTakeaways: Server Actions are 'use server' async functions that run on the server and are called from form actions or client code — no API route needed for internal mutations.
They are public POST endpoints, so authorization and input validation must happen inside the action; never trust form-supplied identity.
After a write, call revalidatePath or revalidateTag (or redirect) — the cache does not invalidate automatically.
useFormStatus gives pending state to child buttons; useActionState threads server-returned errors/success back into the form.
Forms with Server Actions are progressively enhanced: they work without JS, then upgrade to background submissions when hydrated.
